name: Hyacinth Red
lede: Hyacinth Red is the orange-red of the gem once called hyacinth, set down as number 83 in the English version of Werner's nomenclature of colors and used by Darwin on the Beagle.

sections.title: Which hyacinth
sections.body:
The hyacinth in Hyacinth Red is a stone [3]. In Syme's table the color's mineral example is hyacinth, which Baty glosses as jacinth, a silicate mineral [3]. Its other two examples are the red spots of a black-and-red bug and the red patch on the skin of a golden reinette apple [3]. Paterson defines hyacinth red as a reddish orange, and jacinth as a reddish orange that is sometimes yellow [8].

The word has pointed at very different colors. Paterson defines hyacinth blue as a purplish blue popular in the 1930s, and hyacinthine as the purplish blue of the flower, or blue-red, violet or pink [8]. Gage reports that a physician to Emperor Rudolph II, in a book of 1601 on colors, put blue into a five-color scheme under the Latin name *hyacinthinus* [9].

The stone itself is just as unstable. Finlay glosses the jacinth in the biblical list of the heavenly city's foundation stones as sapphire, and the "true hyacinths" in a Roman bride's list of jewels as zircons [10]. In some old texts, then, hyacinth names a blue stone or thread, and in others an orange-red one [8][9][10]. Today the library also holds [[hyacinth-blue]] and [[hyacinth-violet]], both from Ridgway's plates, and Maerz and Paul record the violet from 1388 [11].

sections.title: In Werner's list
sections.body:
Werner devised a list of 54 colors in 1774 so that minerals could be identified by sight, and he kept revising it for some forty years [1]. Hyacinth-red appears in Jameson's English list of 84 colors in 1805 and in both of Syme's editions, of 1814 and 1821 [2]. In the 1821 numbering it is number 83, between Tile Red and [[scarlet]] [3].

Syme built it from scarlet, tinted with lemon yellow and a trace of brown [3]. He then used it as an ingredient in neighbors. Tile Red is hyacinth red dulled with a lot of grey-white and a little scarlet [3]. Brownish Red starts from chocolate red, adds hyacinth red and a touch of chestnut brown, and Brownish Orange is orpiment orange warmed with some hyacinth red and light chestnut [4].

The term also reached the gem trade. By 1813 the English mineralogist John Mawe listed hyacinth red among the tints of [[gem:tourmaline|tourmaline]] in his gem treatise, and used a run of reds, from blood to cherry, crimson and fire, for [[gem:garnet|garnet]] and [[gem:opal|opal]] [5].

sections.title: Darwin's octopus
sections.body:
On 28 January 1832, at the Cape Verde Islands, Darwin described a sea animal that changed color, which he called an octopus [6]. Clouds passed over its body, he wrote, varying from "hyacinth red" to "chesnut brown" [6]. Baty shows that the terms came from Syme's 1821 edition, a copy of which was in the Beagle's library [6].

Syme's colors were meant to be applied to anything in nature. Baty pairs number 83 with a shell from Joseph Banks's *Endeavour* collection and with a protea from a botanical work [7].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
On screen, the library's Hyacinth Red is #A75536, a rust-orange brown, 2.7 units from [[sienna]] and filed with the browns [11]. It is an approximate reading of an aged swatch of Syme's printed color, and Maerz and Paul record the name from 1704 [11]. It is duller and darker than the plain words "reddish orange" suggest [8][11].

Its neighbors in this family are [[brick-red]], [[rust]] and [[terracotta]], and the library's nearest named relative is Sienna [11].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 618 works, 2.6 per cent [12]. The surprise is the date. It peaks in the 1440s, when 13 of 58 paintings carry it, 22 per cent and 8.6 times the archive rate [12]. [[painter:filippo-lippi|Filippo Lippi]] carries it in 6 of his 13 paintings here, [[painter:pontormo|Pontormo]] in 5 of 13 and [[painter:fra-angelico|Fra Angelico]] in 4 of 16 [12]. [[painting:commons-Q3937495|Mantegna's portrait of Carlo de' Medici]], from 1466, is 40 per cent this color [12].

The largest areas are in Indian and Himalayan work [12]. [[painting:cma-314141|A Ragamala page]] from about 1680 is 71 per cent this color [12]. Tibet has it in 13 of 47 works, Nepal in 5 of 25, India in 83 of 721 [12]. Pahari painting carries it 5.5 times as often as the archive average, and Kalighat painting 5.2 times [12].

It most often shares a canvas with rust, 13 times the usual rate, and sienna, 12 times [12]. In the lightness order of a painting it usually sits in the mid-tones, in 65 per cent of cases [12]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [12]. To see the color, look at the red patch on a golden reinette apple, Syme's own example [3].

questions.q: What is the mineral example Syme gave for Hyacinth Red?
Where did Darwin get the term "hyacinth red" for his notes on the Beagle?
In older texts the word hyacinth named only orange-red colors.

openers: Hyacinth Red is named for a gem, not a flower, and the same word once meant blue.
Darwin wrote that a color-changing sea animal passed from hyacinth red to chestnut brown, using terms from a book on the Beagle's shelf.
Look at the red patch on a golden reinette apple: it was Syme's example of number 83.

issues: Hyacinth/jacinth gem identity shifts between texts: stated via Finlay's bracketed glosses (sapphire vs zircon), not asserted for Werner's mineral.
Gage's 1601 physician unnamed (OCR garbled in source).
Swatch is an aged-swatch approximation; Paterson's reddish orange is brighter: said in text.
